blockMcqs.question: What must every LRU cache operation achieve?
options: O(log n) time using a heap
O(n) time but O(1) space
O(1) time only for put
O(1) time for get and put
blockMcqs.explanation: The defining constraint of the LRU cache problem is that both get and put run in O(1), not just one of them.

blockMcqs.question: What role does the HashMap play in the LRU design?
options: It stores items in recency order
It evicts the least-used item
It gives O(1) access to a node by key
It replaces the linked list entirely
blockMcqs.explanation: The HashMap maps key to node for O(1) lookup; the doubly linked list is what tracks recency order.

blockMcqs.question: Why can't a singly linked list remove a node in O(1)?
options: It has no next pointer
It lacks a prev pointer, so finding the predecessor needs a scan
It cannot store key-value pairs
Singly linked lists cannot be traversed
blockMcqs.explanation: Detaching a node requires updating its predecessor's next pointer; without a prev reference, finding that predecessor takes O(n).

blockMcqs.question: Why does the Node store its own key, not just value?
options: To speed up hashing
Keys are required by all languages
To allow duplicate values
So the tail can be deleted from the HashMap on eviction
blockMcqs.explanation: When the tail node is evicted, its key is needed to remove the matching entry from the HashMap.

blockMcqs.question: Why use dummy head and tail sentinel nodes?
options: They store the cache capacity
They speed up HashMap lookups
They remove special-casing for empty or single-node lists
They are required for garbage collection
blockMcqs.explanation: Sentinels guarantee every real node has a non-null prev and next, avoiding edge-case branches for empty or single-item lists.

blockMcqs.question: What must get() do besides returning the value?
options: Delete the node from the map
Move the accessed node to the front of the list
Increment the cache capacity
Rehash the entire map
blockMcqs.explanation: A get counts as a use, so the node must move to the front (most-recently-used position) to keep eviction order correct.

blockMcqs.question: In put(), when does eviction happen?
options: Every time put is called
Only when get has never been called
Only for the very first put
Only when the key is new and the map is at capacity
blockMcqs.explanation: Eviction only triggers when inserting a brand-new key would exceed capacity; updating an existing key never evicts.

blockMcqs.question: What problem do sentinel nodes solve?
options: Slow HashMap resizing
Special-case bugs at empty or boundary list states
Thread-safety violations
Duplicate key collisions
blockMcqs.explanation: Sentinels ensure head.next and tail.prev are always valid, eliminating null checks for empty or single-node lists.

blockMcqs.question: What is the space complexity of an LRU cache?
options: O(n) where n is total requests
O(log capacity)
O(capacity)
blockMcqs.explanation: Space scales with the number of cached items (capacity), not with how many get/put calls occur over time.

blockMcqs.question: How can lock contention be reduced in a concurrent LRU cache?
options: Remove locking entirely
Only lock the HashMap, never the list
Use a single global lock for all reads and writes
Shard into multiple caches by key hash, each with its own lock
blockMcqs.explanation: Sharding by key hash splits load across independent caches with separate locks, cutting contention versus one global lock.

blockMcqs.question: What does LFU evict that LRU would not?
options: The most recently added item
An item with low total use count, even if accessed recently
The largest item in the cache
Items with expired TTLs only
blockMcqs.explanation: LFU tracks frequency, not recency, so it can evict a recently touched but rarely used item that LRU would keep.

blockMcqs.question: What bug results from skipping moveToFront on get?
options: The cache throws an exception
The HashMap loses the entry
Capacity silently doubles
Eviction order becomes incorrect since reads aren't tracked
blockMcqs.explanation: A get is a use; without moving the node to the front, the cache may evict recently read items instead of truly stale ones.
